title: Electric-Field-Induced Second Harmonic Generation at a Reconfigurable LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ Nanojunction
authors: Pubudu Wijesinghe, Melanie Dieterlen, Kyoungjun Lee, Ahmed Omran, Aswini Ramankutty, Chang-Beom Eom, Patrick Irvin, Jeremy Levy
abstract: Electrically tunable nonlinear optical responses at the nanoscale remain challenging to achieve because conventional nonlinear materials lack the combination of large susceptibility, nanoscale confinement, and in situ reconfigurability. Here we report electric-field-induced second harmonic (EFISH) generation from a nanoscale tunnel junction defined by conductive atomic force microscope lithography at the LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ interface. A conducting channel written at the interface is interrupted by a nanoscale insulating gap, across which applied DC bias produces local electric fields exceeding $10^7$ V/m. The SHG signal is spatially localized at the junction, exhibits a quadratic bias dependence described by $I(2ω) \propto |χ^{(2)}_\mathrm{0} + χ^{(3)} E_\mathrm{DC}|^2$ with no hysteresis, a modulation depth exceeding 380% at $|V_\mathrm{DC}| = 1$ V, and shows a two-lobed input-polarization pattern aligned with the junction axis, consistent with EFISH from a centrosymmetric host. Calibration against a BBO reference crystal gives $|χ^{(3)}| \approx 1\times10^{-19}$ m$^2$/V$^2$ at 6 K. These results establish cAFM-written oxide nanojunctions as a reconfigurable platform for nanoscale nonlinear optics in which the junction geometry sets the symmetry of the response and the large field-induced $χ^{(2)}$ of SrTiO$_3$ provides the optical nonlinearity. Because the nonlinearity is both generated and read out within the same nanoscale gap, the junction operates simultaneously as a subwavelength source and a near-field detector of optical nonlinearity.
summary: This paper reports on the observation of electric-field-induced second harmonic generation (EFISH) in a nanoscale LaAlO3/SrTiO3 tunnel junction. By applying a DC bias across the junction, the authors induce a large, tunable nonlinear optical response localized to the nanoscale gap. This establishes the junction as a reconfigurable platform for studying field-controlled nonlinear optics in oxide heterostructures.
main_problem: The challenge is achieving electrically tunable nonlinear optical responses at the nanoscale, as conventional materials lack the necessary combination of large susceptibility, nanoscale confinement, and in situ reconfigurability.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated electric-field-induced second harmonic generation (EFISH) in a nanoscale LaAlO3/SrTiO3 junction, showing a large, tunable signal ($\sim 380\%$ modulation depth) localized to the junction gap.
method: The experiment uses conductive atomic force microscope (cAFM) lithography to create a nanoscale tunnel junction, across which a DC bias is applied while measuring the second harmonic generation (SHG) signal.
model_or_system: The physical system is a reconfigurable LaAlO3/SrTiO3 nanojunction. The nonlinearity is modeled by the SHG intensity $I(2\omega) \propto |\chi^{(2)}_0 + \chi^{(3)} E_{	ext{DC}}|^2$, where the applied DC field $E_{	ext{DC}}$ breaks inversion symmetry and induces the second-order susceptibility $\chi^{(2)}$.
key_observables: SHG intensity vs. DC bias ($V_{	ext{DC}}$), input polarization dependence (two-lobed pattern), and temperature dependence (sharp rise below 50 K).
important_parameters: Estimated third-order susceptibility $|\chi^{(3)}| \approx 1 	imes 10^{-19} 	ext{ m}^2/	ext{V}^2$ at 6 K; junction gap size $\sim 20 	ext{ nm}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the measured response is dominated by the field-induced $\chi^{(2)}$ term, and calibration against BBO is used to quantify $\chi^{(3)}$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device geometry, the strong enhancement of SHG upon applying bias (Fig. 1b), the localization of the signal to the nanoscale gap (Fig. 1d), and the dependence of the signal on bias, polarization, and temperature (Figs. 2, 3, 4).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem, details the cAFM-written junction setup, presents measurements showing bias-dependent, polarization-dependent, and temperature-dependent SHG signals, and concludes by quantifying the field-induced nonlinear susceptibility.
why_interesting: This work demonstrates a solid-state, electrically tunable source of nonlinear optical effects in a highly confined geometry, which is crucial for developing nanoscale quantum optical components.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Device geometry and spatial imaging of the EFISH response. (a) Schematic of the cAFM-written LAO/STO nanojunction with gold contact pads; a conducting nanowire along [100] is interrupted by a ∼20 nm insulating gap, with DC bias VDC applied across the junction. (b) SHG map at VDC = +1 V, showing a localized enhancement at the nanogap (∼80 counts vs. ∼5 counts background). (c) SHG map at zero bias, showing no localized signal above background. (d) Line profiles for both bias conditions; the +1 V profile is fitted by a Gaussian (dashed) with FWHM ≈500 nm, near the diffraction limit for 400 nm light at NA = 0.5.

FIG. 2. Bias dependence of the EFISH signal at the LAO/STO nanojunction. (a) SHG intensity vs. applied DC bias VDC, recorded in forward (blue) and reverse (red) sweeps. Solid curves are fits to Eq. (2), yielding a minimum at Vmin = −50 ± 3 mV consistent between sweeps; the finite signal at VDC = 0 reflects the bias-independent χ(2) 0 contribution, while the dominant quadratic term confirms the EFISH character of the response. (b) Current–voltage characteristic over a wider range, confirming resistive behavior within the ±1 V measurement window (shaded), consistent with negligible carrier transport during the optical measurement.

FIG. 3. (a) Schematic of the polarization-resolved EFISH measurement setup (see also supplementary material Fig. S1). The fundamental beam passes through a half-wave plate (HWP) to set the input polarization angle θ, defined relative to the laboratory Y-axis, with the crystal [100] and [010] axes (dashed green) oriented at ±45◦. The signal is separated by a dichroic beam splitter (DCBS), filtered by a linear polarizer (LP), and measured with a hybrid photomultiplier (HPM). (b) Input polarization dependence of the EFISH signal from the LAO/STO nanojunction at +1 V (blue) and −1 V (red). The signal increases approximately fivefold upon cooling from 290 K to 6 K, a modest enhancement governed by the field-saturated quasi- static soft mode rather than the divergence of its small-signal permit- tivity (see text).
